name: Resumes, LinkedIn and Job Interviews
objectives: Given a real job posting, lay out a one-page resume with contact details, a summary, matching skills and dated experience, on one page, matched to the posting
Given plain job duties, write accomplishment bullets using an action verb, what you did and a result or number, with at least four bullets that are all true
Using your resume, set up a LinkedIn profile with a photo, headline, About section and experience, with no home address or ID numbers and three connection requests sent
Given a behavior interview question, answer with a STAR story: Situation, Task, Action and Result, in one to two minutes with most of the time on Action
When asked a hard question about a gap or a record, give a short, honest answer out loud that says what you have done since, recorded, listened to and improved at least once
At the end of an interview, ask good questions and write a thank-you note, with the note sent within 24 hours

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Building a one-page resume
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Lay out a clean, one-page resume with the right sections in the right order.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real job posting, you will lay out a one-page resume with contact details, a summary, matching skills and dated experience, on one page, matched to the posting.
A resume is a one-page summary of what you can do for an employer. Most hiring managers spend less than a minute on the first look, so the page must be easy to scan: clear headings, plenty of white space, and one simple font such as Calibri or Arial in size 10 to 12.
Use these sections, top to bottom: your name and contact details (phone, a professional email, city and state, and your LinkedIn link if you have one); a two-line summary; skills; work experience, with the newest job first; then education, training and certificates.
Experience is more than paid jobs. Count volunteer work, military service, team captain or coaching roles, church or community work, and jobs or training you did while incarcerated, such as kitchen, maintenance or a trade program. Describe what you did, not where it was, if you prefer.
Change your resume a little for each job. Read the posting, find the skills it asks for, and make sure the words you use match the skills you really have. Many employers use software that searches resumes for those words.
Step by step:
- Open a free word processor such as Google Docs or Microsoft Word, or use a simple resume template.
- Add your name and contact details at the top. Use a professional email, such as one built from your first and last name.
- Write a two-line summary: who you are and what you offer.
- List 6 to 10 skills that match the job posting.
- List experience, newest first: job title, organization, city, dates and 3 to 4 bullets each.
- Add education, training and certificates. Keep it all on one page.
Words to know:
- Resume: a one-page summary of your skills, experience and training that you send when you apply for a job.
- Job posting: the advert that describes a job and what the employer is looking for.
- Applicant tracking system: software many employers use to collect resumes and search them for key words.
Try it now: Find one real job posting you would apply for. Start a new document and build the resume outline for it: your contact details, a two-line summary, six skills that match the posting, and your experience with dates. Leave the bullets for the next lesson.
You can now lay out a one-page resume with the right sections and match it to a job posting.

options: Two lines at the top saying who you are and what you offer
A list of every job you ever had
check.why: A short summary tells the employer quickly what you bring.

check.q: A job posting asks for forklift and inventory skills, which you have. What would you do with your resume?
options: Leave it the same for every job
Add those skills to your skills section and experience
check.why: Matching your resume to the posting shows you fit the job.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing accomplishment bullets
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn plain duties into bullets that show what you achieved.
This lesson builds toward: Given plain job duties, you will write accomplishment bullets using an action verb, what you did and a result or number, with at least four bullets that are all true.
Weak bullets list duties: "Responsible for cleaning." Strong bullets show results: "Cleaned and restocked 12 rooms per shift and passed every weekly inspection." The employer can picture you doing the job well.
A simple formula: action verb + what you did + a result or number. Start with a strong verb such as led, built, trained, fixed, served, organized, reduced or improved. Then add a number if you can: how many people, how much money, how often, or how much faster.
Examples from different lives: "Trained 4 new team members on the store's opening checklist." (retail) "Led a squad of 9 soldiers through daily equipment checks with zero losses." (military) "Captained a varsity team of 22 and organized weekly film study." (athlete) "Prepared meals for 300 people a day in a facility kitchen, meeting every food safety check." (re-entry)
Be truthful. Never make up numbers or job titles. If you are not sure of a number, use a fair estimate with the word "about", or describe the result in words.
Step by step:
- Write down one task you did in a job, team or program.
- Start with an action verb.
- Add what you did and for whom.
- Add a number or a result.
- Read it aloud: does it sound like something you really did?
Words to know:
- Accomplishment bullet: one short line on a resume that shows a result you achieved, not just a duty.
- Action verb: a doing word such as led, built, trained or fixed.
Try it now: Write four accomplishment bullets for your resume using the formula. You can ask an AI assistant: "Make this resume bullet stronger without adding anything that is not true: [your bullet]." Check every word it gives you is true before you keep it.
You can now write accomplishment bullets that start with an action verb and show a result.

check.q: Which is an action verb that starts a strong bullet?
check.why: Bullets start with an action verb that shows what you did.

check.q: Your bullet says "Did customer service." What would you write instead?
options: "Helped about 50 customers a day and handled returns calmly"
check.why: Strong bullets show what you did with a result or number.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Building a LinkedIn profile
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a LinkedIn profile with a photo, headline, About section and experience.
This lesson builds toward: Using your resume, you will set up a LinkedIn profile with a photo, headline, About section and experience, with no home address or ID numbers and three connection requests sent.
LinkedIn is a free professional networking website and app. Employers and recruiters search it for people to hire, and many jobs are posted there. Your profile works like an online resume that people can find.
The most important parts: a clear photo of your face with a plain background; a headline (the line under your name) that says what you do or want to do, such as "Forklift operator | OSHA 10 | Reliable on early shifts"; an About section of three to five sentences in your own voice; and your experience, using the bullets from your resume.
Then build your network. Connect with people you know: former coaches, supervisors, teachers, case managers, people you served with, classmates. Send a short note when you connect. Follow companies you want to work for so you see their job posts.
Keep it professional and safe. Do not post your home address, date of birth or ID numbers. Your profile does not have to mention a record or a gap; it shows your skills.
Step by step:
- Go to linkedin.com or install the official LinkedIn app, and create a free account with a professional email.
- Add a clear, friendly photo.
- Write a headline that says what you do or the job you want.
- Write an About section of three to five sentences.
- Add your experience and skills from your resume.
- Connect with five people you know, with a short note.
Words to know:
- LinkedIn: a free professional networking website and app where people show their work history and employers post jobs.
- Headline: the short line under your name on LinkedIn that says what you do.
- Network: the people you know who can share job leads or speak for your work.
Try it now: Create or update your LinkedIn profile. Write your headline and About section, add one job with your new bullets, and send connection requests with a short note to three people you know.
You can now set up a LinkedIn profile with a photo, headline, About section and experience, and start building your network.

check.q: What does the About section on LinkedIn do?
options: Tells your work story and what you are looking for in a few short lines
check.why: The About section is a short story of your skills and goals.

check.q: You want to connect with a former supervisor on LinkedIn. What would you do?
options: Send a request with a short, friendly note
Send a request with no note and your phone number
Message them asking for a job right away
Wait for them to find you
check.why: A short note reminds them who you are and starts a good connection.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Answering with the STAR method
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Answer a behavior interview question with a short STAR story.
This lesson builds toward: Given a behavior interview question, you will answer with a STAR story: Situation, Task, Action and Result, in one to two minutes with most of the time on Action.
Many interview questions start with "Tell me about a time when...". The employer wants a real example of how you act. The STAR method keeps your answer clear and short.
S is the Situation: where you were and what was going on. T is the Task: what you had to do. A is the Action: what YOU did, step by step. R is the Result: how it ended, with a number if you can, and what you learned.
Example: "Tell me about a time you handled a problem." S: "At my warehouse job, a delivery came in two hours late on a busy day." T: "I had to get it shelved before the store opened." A: "I asked my lead if I could split the team, set up two unloading lines, and checked the labels myself." R: "We finished 15 minutes before opening and nothing was missing."
Prepare five stories before any interview: a time you solved a problem, worked on a team, handled a mistake, dealt with a hard person, and learned something fast. Sports, the military, school, family and programs all give good stories.
Step by step:
- Read the question and pick a real story.
- Situation: one sentence on where and when.
- Task: one sentence on what you had to do.
- Action: two or three sentences on what you did.
- Result: one sentence on how it ended and what you learned.
- Keep the whole answer to about one to two minutes.
Words to know:
- Behavior question: an interview question that asks about a time you did something, to see how you act at work.
- STAR method: a way to answer: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Try it now: Write one STAR story for "Tell me about a time you worked on a team." Use one sentence each for Situation and Task, two or three for Action, and one for Result.
You can now answer a "tell me about a time" question with a clear STAR story.

check.q: What does the S in STAR stand for?
check.why: STAR is Situation, Task, Action and Result.

check.q: You are asked, "Tell me about a time you solved a problem." What would you do?
options: Say "I'm good at solving problems" and stop
Talk for ten minutes about many problems
Say you have never had a problem
Tell one short story: situation, task, what you did and the result
check.why: One short STAR story proves your skill with a real example.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Practicing out loud and answering honestly about a gap or a record
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Practice answers out loud, including a short, honest answer about a gap or a conviction record.
This lesson builds toward: When asked a hard question about a gap or a record, you will give a short, honest answer out loud that says what you have done since, recorded, listened to and improved at least once.
Answers you have only read in your head come out messy. Say them out loud, record yourself on a phone, and listen back. Practice common questions: "Tell me about yourself", "Why do you want this job?", "What are your strengths?", and "Tell me about a time when...". You can ask an AI assistant to play the interviewer and ask you one question at a time.
A gap in work history is common: school, sport, military service, caring for family, health, or incarceration. Keep the answer short and move forward: what the gap was, what you did or learned, and why you are ready now. Example: "I spent two years caring for my mother. I kept my skills up with an online course, and I'm ready to work full time."
If you have a conviction record, do not lie on an application or in an interview. When it is asked about, use a short, honest answer: own it, say what you have done since, and turn to the job. Example: "I made a serious mistake in 2019 and served my time. Since then I finished a forklift certificate and worked 18 months with no missed shifts. I'm ready to bring that reliability here." Do not give long details unless asked.
Know your rights. Under EEOC guidance, an arrest alone is not proof of a crime, and employers should look at the offense, how long ago it was and the job. Many states and cities have "ban the box" or fair chance laws that delay questions about records. Some records can be sealed or expunged; check with a legal aid office or your reentry program. Check the official pages below.
Step by step:
- Write your answer to "Tell me about yourself" in four sentences: now, past, strengths, why this job.
- Record yourself on a phone answering three questions and listen back.
- Write a three-part answer for any gap: what it was, what you did, why you are ready.
- If you have a record: own it, show what you have done since, turn to the job.
- Practice the hard answer out loud until it sounds calm and short.
Words to know:
- Employment gap: a time when you were not working, shown by missing dates on a resume.
- Ban the box: laws in many states and cities that stop employers asking about records on the first job application.
- Expungement: a court process that can clear or seal some records; rules differ by state.
Official sources:
- EEOC: Arrest and conviction records, what job seekers and workers should know
Try it now: Record yourself answering "Tell me about yourself" and one hard question (a gap, a record, or "Why did you leave your last job?"). Listen back. Cut anything that is not needed, then record it again.
You can now practice answers out loud and give a short, honest, forward-looking answer about a gap or a record.

check.q: Why record yourself answering interview questions?
options: So you can hear what to cut and improve
To send it to the employer
check.why: Listening back shows you what to shorten and fix.

check.q: An interviewer asks about a two-year gap when you were incarcerated. What would you say?
options: Give a long story about the case
Give a short, honest answer and say what you have done since
check.why: Short and honest, then focus on what you have done since.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Asking questions and following up
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Ask good questions at the end of an interview and send a thank-you note.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of an interview, you will ask good questions and write a thank-you note, with the note sent within 24 hours.
Near the end, most interviewers ask, "Do you have any questions for us?" Always have two or three ready. It shows interest. Good questions: "What does a great first month look like in this job?", "What do the best people on this team do differently?", "What are the next steps, and when should I expect to hear back?"
Save questions about pay and benefits for when they bring it up or make an offer, unless the posting did not list pay and you need to know. Ask politely.
Within 24 hours, send a short thank-you note by email (or a card for a small local business). Thank them for their time, mention one thing you talked about, and say again why you want the job. Keep it to four or five sentences.
If you do not hear back by the date they gave, send one polite follow-up a few days later. Keep applying to other jobs in the meantime.
Step by step:
- Prepare two or three questions before the interview.
- Ask about the next steps and the timeline.
- Write down the interviewer's name and email.
- Send a short thank-you note within 24 hours.
- Follow up once if you pass the date they gave.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a short, polite message after an interview to thank the employer or ask about next steps.
Try it now: Final task: write a short thank-you note for the interview you practiced for. Then put it all together: your one-page resume, your updated LinkedIn headline and About section, and three recorded STAR answers.
You can now ask good questions at the end of an interview and follow up with a short thank-you note.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds One-page resume Over one page, missing sections, or not matched to the posting. One page with contact details, summary, matching skills and dated experience. Skills and summary use words from the job posting. Accomplishment bullets Bullets list duties only, or anything is not true. At least four true bullets with an action verb and a result or number. Every bullet shows a clear result. LinkedIn profile No headline or About section, or private details shown. Headline and About section match the resume, with no private details. Photo added and three connection requests sent with notes. STAR answers Answers are vague or missing a STAR part. Three recorded STAR answers with all four parts, each one to two minutes. Answers end with a clear result, and most time is on Action. Honest hard answer No answer prepared, or it is long, defensive or untrue. A short, honest answer about a gap or record that turns to what they have done since. Recorded, improved and delivered calmly. Thank-you note No note, or a generic one-word note. A short note with thanks, one thing discussed and why they want the job. Ready to send within 24 hours and has a polite follow-up plan. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does a good thank-you note include?
options: Thanks, one thing you discussed and why you want the job
check.why: Mentioning something you discussed shows real interest.

check.q: At the end of the interview they ask if you have questions. What would you ask?
options: "What are the next steps, and when should I expect to hear back?"
check.why: Asking about next steps shows interest and tells you when to follow up.
